name: Screen Print
basis: why: ink pushed through a mesh one colour at a time, transparent inks multiply; how: threshold layers, multiply, misregistration, mesh hatch

lumenary.blurb: A poster pulled through silk screens, one flat colour per pass. Where inks overlap they mix, and no pass sits quite where it should.

facts.from: Stencil printing in Asia, then commercial presses and art studios
facts.era: Commercial use from the 1900s, pop art in the 1960s

why: Screen printing pushes ink through a mesh, one colour at a time. Cut the picture into brightness bands, print the lightest ink over the darkest regions and add darker inks over smaller areas, and the dark parts receive every ink in turn. Because inks are transparent they multiply, so overlaps create new colours without extra plates.
how: Cut the picture into bands: the lightest ink covers every pixel darker than 0.84, the next everything darker than 0.62, then 0.41, then 0.21.
Print each ink as a separate flat layer.
Combine the layers by multiplication, so yellow over red becomes orange and the full stack is near black.
Shift each pass by its own small random offset for misregistration.
Wobble the thresholds with smooth noise for ragged edges and add a faint cross-hatch from the mesh.
history: Stencil printing through silk or fine mesh was used in East Asia for centuries. Commercial screen printing spread in the early 1900s, and in the 1930s artists proposed the name serigraphy for fine art prints. Andy Warhol made the technique famous in the 1960s, and it is still the main way to print posters, t-shirts and gig bills.
terms: The art term for fine art screen printing.

paragraphs: Screen printing pushes ink through a mesh with a stencil, one colour at a time. The picture is cut into brightness bands, one per ink, from light to dark: the lightest ink (say yellow) covers every pixel darker than 0.84, the next covers everything darker than 0.62, then 0.41, then 0.21. So a dark region receives all the inks, one on top of the other, and a light region only the first.

Inks are transparent and are combined by multiplication, so the overlap of yellow and red is orange and the full stack is nearly black, as in a real print. Three imperfections make it feel physical. Each pass is shifted by its own small random offset (misregistration). The threshold is wobbled by smooth noise, so the edges are slightly ragged. And the ink film is a little uneven, with a faint cross-hatch from the mesh. With fewer inks the program picks a subset (the second and fourth for two, the first, third and fourth for three).

equations.note: Coverage by ink k: o_k is that pass’s offset and r the edge noise.
Multiply overprint; φ is the unevenness of the ink film.
Mesh texture: m is the slider and λ the mesh spacing.
